claim: Ferrari Dacrema et al. name weak/untuned baselines, same-family baseline propagation, and inconsistent evaluation protocols as the specific causes of inflated neural-recommender performance claims.
stance_target: N1: prior work already names classes of unreported implementation confounds in a reality-check paper
scope_conditions: Top-n recommender systems; KDD/SIGIR/WWW/RecSys 2015-2018 deep learning papers
quoted_support: Different factors contribute to such phenomena, including (i) weak baselines; (ii) establishment of weak methods as new baselines; and (iii) difficulties in comparing or reproducing results across papers.

claim: Ferrari Dacrema et al. re-execute published experiments under a controlled protocol (added well-tuned simple baselines, one evaluation setup) and show the published ranking (neural method beats baselines) reverses for 6 of 7 reproducible papers.
stance_target: N1: prior work demonstrates a published ranking change under a controlled re-measurement protocol
scope_conditions: Top-n recommendation, 3 datasets (MovieLens1M, HetRec, Amazon Instant Video)
quoted_support: it turned out that most of the reviewed works can be outperformed at least on some datasets by conceptually and computationally simpler algorithms.
numbers: 6/7 reproducible neural methods beaten by simple baselines
1/7 beat baselines but not a well-tuned non-neural linear ranker

claim: Ferrari Dacrema et al. never perform a quantitative variance decomposition (ANOVA/eta^2) attributing how much of a headline metric each confound explains individually and jointly.
stance_target: N1: the eta^2-style quantitative decomposition of confound contributions is already owned by prior reality-check work
scope_conditions: Full text of the paper, all sections
quoted_support: Our analysis indicates that reproducing published research is still challenging. Furthermore, it turned out that most of the reviewed works can be outperformed at least on some datasets by conceptually and computationally simpler algorithms.

claim: Ferrari Dacrema et al.'s confound vocabulary (baseline strength/tuning, dataset/protocol heterogeneity, code completeness) does not map onto offline MBO's surrogate-model-specific confounds (target scaling, candidate/oracle protocol, ensemble size K, acquisition pessimism beta).
stance_target: residual specific to offline MBO not owned by this paper
scope_conditions: cross-domain comparison, recommender systems vs offline MBO
quoted_support: One first problem lies in the choice of the baselines that are used in the comparisons. Sometimes, baselines are chosen that are too weak in general for the given task and dataset, and sometimes the baselines are not properly fine-tuned.

claim: Ferrari Dacrema et al. identify undocumented/incomplete evaluation protocols and preprocessing as a distinct confound from baseline weakness.
stance_target: N1 sub-shape: naming a candidate/evaluation-protocol confound analogous to offline MBO's candidate/oracle protocol confound
quoted_support: researchers use various types of datasets, evaluation protocols, performance measures, and data preprocessing steps, which makes it difficult to conclude which method is the best across different application scenarios.

claim: The paper's unit of comparison is 'proposed algorithm vs. added baseline', not a crossed factorial of two orthogonal design axes (e.g., surrogate class x optimizer class), so it does not own the crossed-factorial shape of the offline MBO contribution.
quoted_support: Only 7 of them could be reproduced with reasonable effort. For these methods, it however turned out that 6 of them can often be outperformed with comparably simple heuristic methods
